content: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder primarily caused by autoantibodies targeting the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. In less than 5% of cases, the autoantibodies are directed against muscle-specific tyrosine kinase. Plasma exchange is hypothesized to be beneficial for patients with this condition. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of plasma exchange in both the short-term and long-term management of myasthenia gravis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to January 2011. The search also included a review of bibliographies from relevant trial reports and direct communication with one author for additional data. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs involving patients with generalized myasthenia gravis. The trials could assess plasma exchange as a standalone treatment or in combination with corticosteroids or immunosuppressive agents. The primary outcomes were defined as changes in specific muscle scores for exacerbations and changes in functional scales for chronic myasthenia gravis. Four RCTs involving a total of 148 participants were identified. In the first trial, which included 14 participants with moderate to severe myasthenia gravis, there was no statistically significant improvement after one month in the group treated with plasma exchange and prednisone compared to the group treated with prednisone alone. A second trial, a randomized controlled crossover study with 12 participants, also found no significant difference in efficacy between plasma exchange and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) after four weeks. A third trial, involving 87 participants experiencing myasthenia gravis exacerbations, reported no statistically significant difference between plasma exchange and IVIG after two weeks. However, a fourth trial with 35 participants demonstrated a statistically significant benefit of plasma exchange when administered prior to thymectomy. It is important to note that most of these trials, except the third, were at high risk of bias and had limited statistical power. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence from high-quality RCTs to determine whether plasma exchange improves short-term or long-term outcomes in chronic myasthenia gravis or during exacerbations. Nevertheless, case series and observational studies suggest that plasma exchange may provide short-term benefits, particularly in the context of myasthenic crisis. In severe exacerbations, one RCT found no significant difference between plasma exchange and IVIG. Further research is necessary to compare plasma exchange with other short-term treatments, such as IVIG, particularly in the setting of myasthenic crisis or as a preparatory treatment before thymectomy. Additionally, studies are needed to assess the long-term utility of plasma exchange in managing myasthenia gravis.
